subject: physics
title: Bohr Orbits
summary: Put an electron on the right Bohr ring, set its speed and lap time, and count the zeros in a planet’s quantum number.
ncertRef: Section 12.4, Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
concepts: The quantum number of a planet
learningOutcome: The student can find the radius, speed and period of a Bohr orbit from n, and use mvr = nħ to find the huge quantum number of a planet.

levels.title: Hop’s ring
levels.adds: Baseline: the allowed Bohr orbits have radius rₙ = n²a₀ with a₀ = 0.53 Å (Ex 12.7; Example 12.3).
hints: The radius of level n is n² times the radius of the first orbit.
a₀ = 0.53 Å = 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m, so r₂ = 4a₀ and r₃ = 9a₀.
Give the radius in units of 10⁻¹¹ m.

levels.title: Lap’s race
levels.adds: New idea: on level n the speed is v₁/n and the period T = 2πr/v grows as n³ (Ex 12.6).
hints: The speed on level n is v₁/n, with v₁ = 2.19 × 10⁶ m/s.
One lap is 2πr, with r = n²a₀, so T = 2πr/v.

levels.title: Giga’s zeros
levels.adds: Apply it: mvr = nħ, so a planet’s orbit has a quantum number with dozens of zeros (Ex 12.9).
hints: n = mvr/ħ, with ħ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
Multiply m, v and r first, then divide by ħ.
Give log₁₀ n: the exponent of ten.

misconceptions: Bohr’s rule only works for hydrogen and never for a planet
The electron moves faster on higher levels
The radius of level n is n times the radius of the first orbit
